excerpt: A conditional offer telling you to take a pre-sessional English course sounds like a guaranteed path in — but 'guaranteed progression' only covers you if you pass the course's own assessment
content:
You hold a conditional offer: pass a pre-sessional English course and your degree place is secured — no IELTS retake needed. That is the promise of guaranteed progression, and for most students it works exactly as advertised. But the guarantee has conditions of its own, and they live in the small print of two documents: your offer letter and the course's progression rules. This guide explains both.

What 'guaranteed progression' actually means

Guaranteed progression means: if you successfully complete the pre-sessional course — passing its assessed work at the required standard — the university accepts that as meeting your English language condition, and you progress to the degree without re-sitting IELTS. The key words are successfully complete: progression is tied to assessed performance, never to mere attendance.

At a typical university (Manchester's University Centre for Academic English is a well-documented example), assessment means producing written tasks through the course — e.g. four written assignments of 750–1,000 words — plus presentations and seminar participation, marked against the exit standard your degree requires. Universities publish the pass thresholds; you should read them before paying.

The two documents that decide everything

  • Your offer letter — states the exact condition ('attend and pass the 10-week pre-sessional starting 29 June 2027, achieving the required exit standard'). If it says 'attend', ask for the word 'pass' to be clarified in writing.
  • The course progression rules — what happens at each assessment boundary: pass, borderline (resit) and fail outcomes. Ask the admissions office for this document by name.

What happens if you fail the pre-sessional course

Failure is uncommon but real, and the consequences differ by university:

  1. Resit window — many courses allow one reassessment of failed tasks within the course, which is the cheapest fix.
  2. Longer pre-sessional or deferral — some universities offer transfer to a longer course (if timelines allow) or deferral to the next intake on condition of a stronger English result.
  3. Offer withdrawn — the hard outcome: no progression, and you reapply or pivot to another university. Your tuition deposit refund depends on the refund policy you signed, not on goodwill.

Ask directly: 'What percentage of students progress each year, and what exactly happens to those who do not?' Universities track these numbers internally; a confident answer is a good sign.

Flexible start dates and online options

Pre-sessional courses are usually 6, 10 or 20 weeks long, chosen by the gap between your current IELTS score and the target. Many universities now run online pre-sessional courses with multiple start dates, which matters if your visa, results or funding arrive late: ask whether the online version carries identical progression rights to the face-to-face course — at some universities it does; at others the online route is assessment-restricted. Also confirm the course is CAS-compatible: a pre-sessional that issues its own CAS covers the course plus degree only if the university sponsors the combined visa.

The 6 questions to ask before you pay

  1. Is my progression guaranteed on passing, or subject to a further internal test?
  2. What are the exit assessments and the pass thresholds for my degree?
  3. What happens if I fail — resit, longer course, deferral or withdrawal?
  4. Are there flexible or online start dates, and do they carry the same progression rights?
  5. Does the course fee include accommodation, and what is the refund policy?
  6. What percentage of students progressed last year?

Costs and alternatives

Pre-sessional fees typically run £2,000–£6,000 depending on length — our full cost guide compares price per week and hidden extras. Before committing, check the alternatives: some universities waive English tests on a Medium of Instruction (MOI) letter from your previous university — see our MOI-waiver university list — and others accept cheaper tests like PTE or Duolingo. A pre-sessional is the right choice when your IELTS gap is small and your start date is close; it is the wrong choice when a one-sitting retake could clear the condition outright.

faqs.question: Does a pre-sessional English course guarantee progression to my degree?
faqs.answer: Guaranteed progression means the university accepts the course's own exit assessments as meeting your English condition — so progression is guaranteed only if you pass those assessments at the required standard, not by attendance alone. Check your offer letter and the course progression rules for the exact conditions.

faqs.question: I've been given a conditional offer that requires a pre-sessional English course — how do these work?
faqs.answer: You take an intensive English course (commonly 6, 10 or 20 weeks, chosen by the gap between your current IELTS and the target) before the degree starts. You complete assessed written and spoken work; passing at the required standard clears your English condition without retaking IELTS. The offer letter states the course, its dates and the exit standard you need.

faqs.question: What happens if I fail my pre-sessional English course?
faqs.answer: It depends on the university: most offer one reassessment within the course, some allow transfer to a longer course or deferral to a later intake, and in the worst case the offer is withdrawn. Progression and pass-rate statistics exist internally — ask admissions what happened to students who failed last year before you pay.

faqs.question: Can I take a pre-sessional English course online with flexible start dates?
faqs.answer: Many UK universities now run online pre-sessional courses with multiple start dates. Confirm two things before enrolling: that the online route carries identical guaranteed-progression rights to the on-campus course, and how the course interacts with your student visa CAS if you need one for the degree.

faqs.question: Is a pre-sessional course cheaper than retaking IELTS?
faqs.answer: No — a pre-sessional typically costs £2,000–£6,000 against roughly £200 for an IELTS sitting. The pre-sessional makes sense when your score gap is too large to close with one retake, when you need academic English preparation anyway, or when your degree start date is too close for another test cycle. See our pre-sessional cost guide for the full comparison.
